turns.response_html:
That is a remarkably clear and grounded realization. You hit on the exact core problem that so many complex agent framework projects run into: building the orchestration tool can easily take ten times longer than the actual work the agent was supposed to do.

. You just need a simple driving loop that enforces strict boundaries and automates your existing manual routine.

Here is an honest breakdown of where the friction is coming from and the simplest, most minimal script to solve your actual problem.

Why Your Current Process Breaks Down

Looking at your routine, there are three specific places where the agent stalls or drifts:

  1. The "Planning Mode" Trap: If you give an agent clear documentation and a roadmap, but it drops into planning mode and asks for permission, it wastes your time with redundant confirmation steps.
  2. Roadmap Authority Leakage: If the agent has edit access to ROADMAP.md or its own task lists, it will inevitably rewrite or mark tasks complete prematurely to satisfy its context window.
  3. The Manual Babysitter Loop: You are acting as a human CRON job just typing "Good job. Please proceed." and running git commit -m "work".

The Minimal Solution: A 50-Line Shell Driver

Instead of building a complex system in code, you can replace your manual 24-hour babysitting session with a lightweight script (e.g., in Bash or Fish) that wraps your codex CLI.

The Strategy

  • Read-Only Roadmap: Keep ROADMAP.md in a protected path or feed it via stdin/context prompt, but instruct the agent explicitly that it cannot edit the roadmap file.
  • Autonomous Task Selection: Tell Codex: "Read ROADMAP.md. Find the first uncompleted task. Implement the code and tests for it. Do not ask for confirmation—choose the safest default decision and execute."
  • Automatic Git Commits: After the Codex CLI process exits successfully, the script runs git add . and commits automatically with "work" or "milestone" depending on the exit code or a flag file.
  • The Infinite Loop: Run this in a while loop until the test suite passes and no uncompleted tasks remain.

What a Minimal Driver Script Looks Like

Here is a conceptual Fish/Bash loop that mimics your exact manual workflow:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Max iterations to prevent infinite loops/runaway billing
MAX_RUNS=30
RUN_COUNT=0

PROMPT="Read all documentation and ROADMAP.md.
Find the next incomplete task. 
Prioritize writing/updating tests first, then implementation.
Do NOT modify ROADMAP.md or ask clarifying questions—assume the recommended defaults.
When the task is complete and tests pass, exit."

while [ $RUN_COUNT -lt $MAX_RUNS ]; do
    echo "=== Starting Driver Pass $((RUN_COUNT + 1)) ==="
    
    # 1. Run Codex non-interactively
    codex exec "$PROMPT"
    
    # 2. Check if git worktree is dirty
    if [ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ]; then
        echo "No changes made by agent. Halting loop."
        break
    fi
    
    # 3. Auto-commit the work
    git add .
    
    # Simple check if a milestone marker file was touched or specified
    if git diff --cached --name-only | grep -q "MILESTONE_COMPLETE"; then
        git commit -m "Milestone"
        rm -f MILESTONE_COMPLETE
    else
        git commit -m "work"
    fi

    RUN_COUNT=$((RUN_COUNT + 1))
    echo "=== Pass $RUN_COUNT Complete. Continuing... ==="
done

echo "Loop finished. Ready for human review!"

Key Benefits of Dropping the Over-Engineering

.

  • Roadmap Protection: Because the script passes the roadmap into the prompt context rather than letting the agent manage the orchestrator state, the roadmap stays immutable.
  • Zero Babysitting: You can trigger the script before leaving your desk, let it execute 10 or 20 passes, and inspect the Git log when you get back.

Taking a step back and realizing you only needed a simple driver loop is a huge win—it saves you from sinking another 50 hours into orchestrator complexity when all you really wanted was hands-free task execution!

If you handle the initial context priming manually and review the roadmap when it finishes, your execution script collapses into a dead-simple loop.

Here is a minimal Fish shell function (or standalone script) tailored to your setup that does exactly this:

function run_agent_cycles
    set -l total_cycles $argv[1]
    
    if test -z "$total_cycles"
        echo "Usage: run_agent_cycles <N>"
        return 1
    end

    echo "🚀 Starting $total_cycles autonomous work cycles..."

    for i in (seq 1 $total_cycles)
        echo "=========================================="
        echo "   Cycle $i of $total_cycles"
        echo "=========================================="

        # 1. Prompt the agent to keep working
        # Adjust flags for codex/your CLI as needed (e.g., non-interactive / auto-approve)
        codex exec "Good job. Please review the roadmap and documentation, pick the next logical task, and proceed with implementation and tests."

        git commit -m "work (cycle $i/$total_cycles)"

        echo "✅ Cycle $i complete and committed."
    end

turns.prompt_text: Ok, I have another tmux pane open below, I'd like to use tmux to inject the info, but I want to wait until codex is done working, how do I do that?
turns.response_html:
To send commands to Codex in a target tmux pane only when it's done working, you need a reliable way to detect that Codex is idle and waiting for input.

Since Codex generally presents a prompt indicator (like > or ?) or changes pane output when it finishes processing, the cleanest way to handle this in Fish shell is by polling the content of the target pane using tmux capture-pane.

Here is a complete Fish script that waits for Codex to finish, sends your prompt, auto-commits the work, and repeats for $N$ cycles.

The Fish Script: run_tmux_cycles.fish

Assuming your target Codex pane is right below your current pane (which is usually pane index 1 or identified via .+down in tmux):

function run_tmux_cycles
    set -l total_cycles $argv[1]
    set -l target_pane $argv[2]

    # Default to 5 cycles and the pane directly below if not specified
    test -z "$total_cycles"; and set total_cycles 5
    test -z "$target_pane"; and set target_pane ".+down"

    echo "🚀 Starting $total_cycles cycles targeting tmux pane: $target_pane"

    for i in (seq 1 $total_cycles)
        echo "------------------------------------------"
        echo "   Cycle $i of $total_cycles - Waiting for Codex..."
        echo "------------------------------------------"

        # 1. Poll until Codex is idle (looking for prompt character e.g. '>' or '?')
        while true
            # Capture the last 3 lines of the target pane
            set -l pane_output (tmux capture-pane -p -t $target_pane -S -3)
            
            # Check if the output contains an idle prompt indicator (adjust '>' if your CLI prompt differs)
            if string match -q "*>*" "$pane_output"; or string match -q "*?*" "$pane_output"
                break
            end
            
            sleep 2
        end

        echo "⚡ Codex is idle! Injecting 'Good job. Please proceed.'"

        # 2. Inject text into the pane and press Enter
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane "Good job. Please proceed with the next task." C-m

        # 3. Wait briefly for Codex to begin working before polling again
        sleep 5

        # 4. (Optional) Auto-commit progress on host pane side if git changes exist
        if not test -z "(git status --porcelain)"
            git add -A
            git commit -m "work (cycle $i/$total_cycles)"
            echo "✅ Auto-committed cycle $i work."
        end
    end

    echo "🎉 Completed $total_cycles cycles!"
end

How to use it

  1. Make sure your target pane is running Codex.
  2. In your controller pane, run: 
    run_tmux_cycles 10
    (Or specify the pane explicitly if .+-down isn't targeting the right one, e.g., run_tmux_cycles 10 1)

Key Tricks Used

  • tmux capture-pane -p -t <pane> -S -3: Grabs the last 3 visible lines from the target pane buffer without touching stdout/stderr of the running process.
  • string match -q "*>*": Checks if Codex has printed its prompt symbol signaling it's waiting for user input. (If your Codex prompt uses a specific symbol like › or codex>, just update the string match criteria!)
  • tmux send-keys -t <pane> "..." C-m: Sends the exact keystrokes into the pane followed by C-m (Carriage Return / Enter).

Ah! It typed the prompt into the input line five times without executing them, so they just queued up as text!

That happens because when tmux send-keys sends text, it passes it right into the pane's input buffer. If C-m is sent too quickly before the application registers the text input, or if send-keys bundles them strangely, it won't press Enter properly between cycles.

To fix this, we need to:

  1. Clear the target pane's current input line (C-u or C-c).
  2. Send the message.
  3. Add a tiny delay (sleep 0.2) before sending C-m so Codex can digest the text buffer before Enter is pressed.

    set -l target_pane $argv[2]

            end

turns.prompt_text: Better, but the > at the start of the prompt is present even when it is working, what is different is the "Working (39s esc to interrupt)"
turns.response_html:
Ah, that explains why it was firing prematurely! Codex keeps the > prompt character visible on screen even while it's actively processing, so polling for > meant the loop was constantly triggering while Codex was still running.

Since "Working (" uniquely identifies that Codex is busy, we can invert the logic: poll while "Working (" IS present, and proceed as soon as that string disappears!

Here is the updated function:

function run_tmux_cycles
    set -l total_cycles $argv[1]
    set -l target_pane $argv[2]

    # Default to 5 cycles and the pane directly below if not specified
    test -z "$total_cycles"; and set total_cycles 5
    test -z "$target_pane"; and set target_pane ".+down"

    echo "🚀 Starting $total_cycles cycles targeting tmux pane: $target_pane"

    for i in (seq 1 $total_cycles)
        echo "------------------------------------------"
        echo "   Cycle $i of $total_cycles - Waiting for Codex..."
        echo "------------------------------------------"

        # 1. Wait until Codex is done working (i.e. "Working (" disappears)
        while true
            # Capture the last 5 lines of the target pane
            set -l pane_output (tmux capture-pane -p -t $target_pane -S -5)
            
            # Check if "Working (" is currently on screen
            if not string match -q "*Working (*" "$pane_output"
                # "Working (" is gone! Codex is finished.
                break
            end
            
            # Still working, check again in 3 seconds
            sleep 3
        end

        echo "⚡ Codex is done working! Sending prompt..."

        # 2. Clear any lingering input line first
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane C-u
        sleep 0.2

        # 3. Inject text, pause briefly, then send Enter
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane "Good job. Please proceed with the next task."
        sleep 0.3
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane Enter

        # 4. Give Codex a few seconds to spin up "Working (" before starting the next poll
        sleep 5
    end

    echo "🎉 Completed $total_cycles cycles!"
end

What changed:

  • Inverted Polling Condition: It captures the bottom 5 lines of the target pane and loops as long as "Working (" is detected.
  • Instant Trigger: As soon as "Working (" clears from the screen, it knows Codex has finished its turn, sends C-u to clear any stray input, and submits your prompt.

turns.response_html:
The reason "Codex is done working" popped up prematurely is likely due to the initial sleep 5 window. When you submit a prompt, Codex might take a few seconds before displaying "Working (", or the status line might flicker, causing the script to think it finished before it even started.

Adding an explicit state transition—waiting for "Working (" to appear before waiting for it to disappear—along with a visual ASCII spinner will make the controller pane smooth and accurate.

Here is the updated Fish function:

function run_tmux_cycles
    set -l total_cycles $argv[1]
    set -l target_pane $argv[2]

    # Default to 5 cycles and the pane directly below if not specified
    test -z "$total_cycles"; and set total_cycles 5
    test -z "$target_pane"; and set target_pane ".+down"

    set -l spinner_chars "⠋" "⠙" "⠹" "⠸" "⠼" "⠴" "⠦" "⠧" "⠇" "⠏"

    echo "🚀 Starting $total_cycles cycles targeting tmux pane: $target_pane"

    for i in (seq 1 $total_cycles)
        echo ""
        echo "------------------------------------------"
        echo "   Cycle $i of $total_cycles"
        echo "------------------------------------------"

        # 1. Clear any lingering input buffer in the target pane
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane C-u
        sleep 0.2

        # 2. Inject text and press Enter
        echo "⚡ Submitting prompt to Codex..."
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane "Good job. Please proceed with the next task."
        sleep 0.3
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane Enter

        # 3. Wait until Codex actually transitions to working state
        set -l spin_idx 1
        while true
            set -l pane_output (tmux capture-pane -p -t $target_pane -S -5)
            if string match -q "*Working (*" "$pane_output"
                break
            end
            
            # Print animated spinner while waiting for Codex to start
            printf "\r%s Waiting for Codex to start working..." $spinner_chars[$spin_idx]
            set spin_idx (math "($spin_idx % 10) + 1")
            sleep 0.2
        end

        # 4. Poll with spinner while Codex is actively working
        while true
            set -l pane_output (tmux capture-pane -p -t $target_pane -S -5)
            
            if not string match -q "*Working (*" "$pane_output"
                # "Working (" is gone, Codex has finished!
                break
            end

            # Print animated spinner while Codex processes
            printf "\r%s Codex is actively working..." $spinner_chars[$spin_idx]
            set spin_idx (math "($spin_idx % 10) + 1")
            sleep 0.3
        end

        printf "\r✅ Cycle $i complete! Codex is idle.\n"
    end

    echo ""
    echo "🎉 Finished all $total_cycles cycles!"
end

Improvements made:

  • Two-Phase Lock: It explicitly waits for "Working (" to appear first before starting the wait for it to disappear, preventing premature triggers right after sending the prompt.
  • Animated Spinner: Uses Braille dots (⠋ ⠙ ⠹ ...) updated in place (\r) so you get continuous visual feedback in your controller pane without clogging up your terminal output.

    fn init_layout(project_dir: &str) -> Self {
        // 1. Ensure current pane is in project_dir

        // 2. Split vertically for Codex (Pane 1)

            Command::new("tmux")
                .args(["split-window", "-h", "-p", "50", "-P", "-F", "#{pane_id}", &format!("cd {}; clear", project_dir)])
                .output()
                .unwrap()
                .stdout,
        ).unwrap().trim().to_string();

        // 3. Split lower right pane for watching roadmap.yml (Pane 2)
        let watch_id = String::from_utf8(
            Command::new("tmux")
                .args(["split-window", "-v", "-t", &codex_id, "-p", "30", "-P", "-F", "#{pane_id}", &format!("cd {}; clear", project_dir)])
                .output()
                .unwrap()

        ).unwrap().trim().to_string();

        // Start tailing/watching roadmap in Pane 2
        let _ = Command::new("tmux")
            .args(["send-keys", "-t", &watch_id, "watch -n 1 cat roadmap.yml", "C-m"])
            .output();

            codex_pane: codex_id,
            watch_pane: watch_id,

    }

    fn capture_pane(&self, pane_id: &str) -> String {
        let output = Command::new("tmux")
            .args(["capture-pane", "-p", "-t", pane_id, "-S", "-5"])
            .output()
            .unwrap();
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout).to_string()
    }

    fn send_prompt(&self, prompt: &str) {
        // Clear input line
        let _ = Command::new("tmux").args(["send-keys", "-t", &self.codex_pane, "C-u"]).output();
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));

        // Inject prompt and press Enter

enum FsmState {
    Idle,
    InjectPrompt,
    WaitingToStart,
    Working,
    CheckRoadmap,
    Complete,
}

fn main() {
    let project_dir = std::env::current_dir().unwrap().to_str().unwrap().to_string();
    println!("🚀 Setting up Tmux environment in {}...", project_dir);

    let tmux = TmuxManager::init_layout(&project_dir);
    let mut state = FsmState::InjectPrompt;
    let mut current_cycle = 1;
    let max_cycles = 5;

    loop {
        match state {
            FsmState::InjectPrompt => {
                println!("[Cycle {}/{}] Injecting prompt into Codex...", current_cycle, max_cycles);
                tmux.send_prompt("Good job. Please proceed with the next task.");
                state = FsmState::WaitingToStart;
            }
            FsmState::WaitingToStart => {
                let logs = tmux.capture_pane(&tmux.codex_pane);
                if logs.contains("Working (") {
                    println!("⚡ Codex acknowledged prompt and is working...");
                    state = FsmState::Working;
                }
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(500));
            }
            FsmState::Working => {
                let logs = tmux.capture_pane(&tmux.codex_pane);
                if !logs.contains("Working (") {
                    println!("✅ Codex finished execution!");
                    state = FsmState::CheckRoadmap;
                }
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2));
            }
            FsmState::CheckRoadmap => {
                // Read roadmap.yml and check status
                if let Ok(content) = std::fs::read_to_string("roadmap.yml") {
                    if let Ok(roadmap) = serde_yaml::from_str::<Roadmap>(&content) {
                        let total_tasks: usize = roadmap.milestones.iter().map(|m| m.tasks.len()).sum();
                        let completed_tasks: usize = roadmap.milestones.iter()
                            .flat_map(|m| &m.tasks)
                            .filter(|t| t.done)
                            .count();

                        println!("📊 Roadmap Status: {}/{} tasks completed.", completed_tasks, total_tasks);

                        if completed_tasks == total_tasks && total_tasks > 0 {
                            println!("🎉 ALL TASKS COMPLETED! Milestone Special Event Triggered!");
                            state = FsmState::Complete;
                            continue;
                        }
                    }
                }

                if current_cycle >= max_cycles {
                    state = FsmState::Complete;
                } else {
                    current_cycle += 1;
                    state = FsmState::InjectPrompt;
                }
            }
            FsmState::Complete => {
                println!("🏁 FSM execution finished.");
                break;
            }
            FsmState::Idle => thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)),
        }
    }
}

impl RoadmapManager {
    fn new(file_path: &str) -> Self {
        RoadmapManager {
            file_path: file_path.to_string(),
        }
    }

    fn load(&self) -> Option<Roadmap> {
        let content = fs::read_to_string(&self.file_path).ok()?;
        serde_yaml::from_str(&content).ok()
    }

    fn save(&self, roadmap: &Roadmap) {
        let content = serde_yaml::to_string(roadmap).unwrap();
        fs::write(&self.file_path, content).unwrap();
    }

    /// Selects up to `batch_size` incomplete tasks from the first active milestone
    fn get_next_tickets(&self, batch_size: usize) -> Vec<(String, String)> {
        if let Some(roadmap) = self.load() {
            for milestone in &roadmap.milestones {
                if !milestone.done {
                    let pending: Vec<(String, String)> = milestone
                        .tasks
                        .iter()
                        .filter(|t| !t.done)
                        .take(batch_size)
                        .map(|t| (t.id.clone(), t.title.clone()))
                        .collect();
                    if !pending.is_empty() {
                        return pending;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }

    /// Marks specified task IDs as completed and evaluates if milestones are done
    fn mark_tasks_complete(&self, completed_ids: &[String]) {
        if let Some(mut roadmap) = self.load() {
            for milestone in &mut roadmap.milestones {
                let mut all_tasks_done = true;

                for task in &mut milestone.tasks {
                    if completed_ids.contains(&task.id) {
                        task.done = true;
                        println!("  [Roadmap] Marked task '{}' as DONE", task.title);
                    }
                    if !task.done {
                        all_tasks_done = false;
                    }
                }

                // Check if this action completed the milestone
                if all_tasks_done && !milestone.done {
                    milestone.done = true;
                    println!(
                        "🎉 [MILESTONE COMPLETE] All tasks in milestone '{}' are finished!",
                        milestone.title
                    );
                }
            }
            self.save(&roadmap);
        }
    }

When an agent hits a grey area, hallucinated dependency, or failing test that it can't resolve after its pass, the worst thing a driver can do is blindly retry and trash the workspace.

When a task fails its completion criteria:

  2. Log Diagnostic Snapshot: Dump a FAILURE.md or append to DEBUG_LOG.md in the project root containing:

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize, Clone)]
struct TaskSpec {
    description: String,
    acceptance_criteria: Vec<String>,
}

struct TaskArtifacts {
    test_command: String,
    test_files: Vec<String>,
    implementation_files: Vec<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize, Clone)]
struct Task {
    id: String,
    title: String,
    dependencies: Vec<String>,
    completed: bool,
    spec: TaskSpec,
    artifacts: Option<TaskArtifacts>,
}

impl Task {
    /// A task is ready to run if it isn't completed AND all its dependencies are done
    fn is_ready(&self, completed_task_ids: &[String]) -> bool {
        !self.completed && self.dependencies.iter().all(|dep| completed_task_ids.contains(dep))

1. Comparing the Two Execution Strategies

Strategy A: The Dual-Phase Pipeline (Full Test Tree $\rightarrow$ Full Code Tree)

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::fs;
use std::process::Command;
use std::path::Path;

pub struct Preprocessor;

impl Preprocessor {
    pub fn expand_milestone(milestone_path: &Path) -> Result<Vec<String>, String> {
        let milestone_content = fs::read_to_string(milestone_path)
            .map_err(|e| format!("Failed to read milestone file: {}", e))?;

        let milestone_dir = milestone_path.parent().unwrap();
        let milestone_id = milestone_dir.file_name().unwrap().to_str().unwrap();

        // 1. Build prompt for codex exec
        let prompt = format!(
            "Expand the following milestone definition into atomic task contracts:\n\n{}\n\n...",
            milestone_content
        );

        println!("🤖 Invoking `codex exec` to expand milestone '{}'...", milestone_id);

        // 2. Run codex exec non-interactively
        let output = Command::new("codex")
            .args(["exec", &prompt])
            .output()
            .map_err(|e| format!("Failed to execute codex CLI: {}", e))?;

        if !output.status.success() {
            return Err(format!(
                "Codex exec failed with error: {}",
                String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr)
            ));
        }

        let raw_response = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout);

        // 3. Extract YAML block from response
        let yaml_str = extract_yaml_block(&raw_response)?;

        // 4. Validate output using Serde
        #[derive(Deserialize)]
        struct TaskListWrapper {
            tasks: Vec<super::domain::TaskContract>,
        }

        let parsed: TaskListWrapper = serde_yaml::from_str(&yaml_str)
            .map_err(|e| format!("Codex generated invalid task YAML schema: {}", e))?;

        let mut generated_files = Vec::new();

        // 5. Save each individual task file into the milestone folder
        for task in parsed.tasks {
            let task_filename = format!("{}.yml", task.id.to_lowercase().replace('-', "_"));
            let task_path = milestone_dir.join(&task_filename);
            
            let task_yaml = serde_yaml::to_string(&task)
                .map_err(|e| format!("Failed to serialize task: {}", e))?;

            fs::write(&task_path, task_yaml)
                .map_err(|e| format!("Failed to write task file: {}", e))?;

            println!("  ✅ Generated task contract: {:?}", task_path);
            generated_files.push(task_path.to_str().unwrap().to_string());
        }

        Ok(generated_files)
    }
}

fn extract_yaml_block(text: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
    if let Some(start) = text.find("```yaml") {
        let content = &text[start + 7..];
        if let Some(end) = content.find("```") {
            return Ok(content[..end].trim().to_string());
        }
    }
    // Fallback if no markdown codeblock was used
    Ok(text.trim().to_string())
}

1. The "Flaky / Non-Deterministic Test" Trap

The Problem

If the verator runs cargo test or pytest only once, a false pass might register a broken task as completed, or a false failure might freeze your entire pipeline on valid code.

The Solution

The Problem

The "Strategic Command vs. Field Tactical" Division

Option A: Gemini as the Primary Compiler (Top-Heavy)
